There's no accounting for luck, and some fields are very competitive or require a lot of specialized knowledge (especially physical engineering fields).

That aside, the question is are you comfortable where you are, at your current income level, for you personally with your job, disregarding what anyone else says or considers. That should be the deciding factor on what you want to do. When it comes to getting a degree, it can't hurt you (unless you're taking the wrong degree for your desired job which should be an obvious given). They're effectively a certification and an indicator that you have the willpower to work through something to completion (though in your case all the work you've already done is an indicator of that, at least to me) but in the corporate world, management still like to see their shiny pieces of paper.

While the money issue is something to consider, you maybe able to get significant financing aid through your company. A lot of companies will give tuition reimbursement and flexible scheduling that can help you work around work. That's something you'll have to find out if you haven't already. It's good that you started at a two-year school, as it allows you the potential to transfer your credit to another school, if you so desire, (I saved well over half my tuition doing that) provided that the school accepts that transfer credit. It's something to look into if you haven't considered it as some degree programs are better suited for a job than others.

As for your family, they are negging you; which is emotional blackmail and abusive. If you can, you should put some distance between yourself and them for a while. Their behavior is a very poor reason to embark on a such a time intensive project like this and if they're the kind of people who shit on you for not doing something they want, then you're probably better off without them.

Either way, whatever you decide, your degree may or may not benefit you fiscally. Sometimes life just doesn't work out the way we expect, but if you do gain anything from finishing your degree, even if it's just personal satisfaction, then you've gotten something worthwhile out of it.
